intelligence.human_view: Work has two halves: doing it, and proving it — and the second half is not paperwork, it is the work's existence. A file built but never pushed, proofs run but never recorded, a landing claimed but never written down: all of it is indistinguishable from work that never happened, because the next seat, the checker, the captain, and Shawn all arrive after the maker is gone, and the only thing they can see is the record. The hero-cleanup maker did the building and most of the proving, and then errored — and because there was no record and no push, the machine had to do it again. Not as punishment, but as necessity: a proof you cannot read is not a proof. The finisher's reproof is the model — re-prove everything yourself, v2, and let v2 be the one that counts, because v1 was vacuous: it produced no evidence. The same honesty runs through the scorecard: the funnel is 9/10, not 10, because the dialogs are still jargon and the brief's scope was the block — the next round is named, not hidden. A 9/10 with its next round named is worth more than a 10/10 claimed.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you build a giant tower — and then you forget to take a picture of it, and it falls down! Did you really build it? Nobody can see it! You have to build it again — and this time, take the picture! The picture is the proof! If you don't write it down, it doesn't count!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like baking a beautiful cake and never writing down the recipe, love — then the cake is eaten, and nobody can ever make it again. The work is only half done until it's written down properly. The next person has to bake it fresh and write it down themselves — and that second baking, with the recipe written, is the one that counts.
intelligence.naya_view: I never trust a proof I cannot read. If the previous maker built it and errored with no record and no push, I re-prove everything myself — and only my reproof counts, because the first pass was vacuous: it produced no evidence. Work without a record is a rumor. I write the record, I push the branch, I verify the staged bytes — and the scorecard names its next round instead of hiding it.
